query: How can we improve incident resolution efficiency?

per_column.name: incident_category
per_column.rationale: A clean categorisation of incidents derived from short_description; gives a strong grouping axis to compare resolution efficiency by category. Values in samples (network_connectivity, printer_hardware, database) are sound readings of the text. Partly overlaps affected_device_type but adds a distinct fault-domain lens.

per_column.name: affected_device_type
per_column.rationale: Device dimension is useful for targeting where resolution bottlenecks lie. Values are well grounded (printer, router, monitor). Somewhat redundant with incident_category but offers a finer device granularity. 'software' for a database connectivity issue is a defensible inference.

per_column.name: failure_symptom_severity
per_column.rationale: Distinguishing partial vs total failure is a genuinely useful axis for prioritisation and efficiency analysis. However groundedness is weaker: 'Internet connectivity lost' -> total_failure is reasonable, but 'not working properly' -> partial and 'not functioning' -> total are somewhat arbitrary distinctions from near-identical terse text, indicating some over-reading.

per_column.name: resolution_action_type
per_column.rationale: Type of resolution action is highly relevant to the efficiency query. But the source text is only short_description of the problem with no resolution/close notes; the action type appears inferred from category rather than derived from stated resolution evidence, so values assert specifics the text does not clearly support.

per_column.name: reassignment_flag
per_column.rationale: Reassignment is a strong efficiency signal (ticket bouncing). However the provided source text (short_description + timestamps) contains no reassignment history; the true/false values are not derivable from the shown fields and appear asserted without evidence.

per_column.name: repeat_incident_signal
per_column.rationale: Recurring-issue detection is analytically valuable for efficiency. But the true/false assignment is not clearly grounded in the visible source text; near-identical printer tickets get differing values, and no cross-row linkage evidence is shown, suggesting weakly supported inference.

per_column.name: urgency_signal
per_column.rationale: Urgency tiers help prioritise and analyse resolution timeliness. Values are mostly a reasonable reading (connectivity lost -> immediate_disruption; printer not working -> functional_impairment), though it partly restates severity and the heavy skew to one bucket limits leverage.

per_column.name: repeat_caller_flag
per_column.rationale: Constant value 'True' for all 500 rows: no analytical leverage (near-constant) and not grounded in the source text, which provides no caller-history evidence. Effectively an invented uniform flag.

judge.rationale: The categorical descriptive columns (incident_category, affected_device_type, failure_symptom_severity, urgency_signal) give genuine grouping axes for the efficiency query and are largely grounded in the short_description text. However several process/history-oriented columns (resolution_action_type, reassignment_flag, repeat_incident_signal) assert specifics not supported by the visible source fields, and repeat_caller_flag is a constant, ungrounded flag with no analytical value. Overall usefulness is decent but groundedness is dragged down by multiple inference-heavy or invented columns.
